name: Gorowa
confidence_why: Harvey's 2018 SOAS dissertation, the only modern first-hand description of Gorwaa, states the rule with examples (stress on the first syllable by default, on the penult when its vowel is long, on the final syllable when the penult is short and the final carries high tone), and Harvey and Mreta 2016, the same author writing on Swahili loanwords, fits that rule (a lengthened penult takes the stress) while no other source describes Gorwaa stress at all.

new_statements.quote: [p. 1, Abstract] "Vowels are very often lengthened on the stressed (penultimate) syllable." [p. 7] "Vowel-Lengthening. Lengthened vowels will be on the stressed (i.e. penultimate) syllable" (10a [filimbi] -> [fili:mbi] 'flute', 10b [gazeti] -> [gase:ti] 'newspaper', 10c [kalamu] -> [kala:mu] 'pen'). [p. 7] "Words in Gorwaa and Iraqw cannot feature a stressed final vowel which is long, as such, words adopted from Swahili featuring a stressed final vowel will be repaired by the suffix /-ɁX/, where X is a short vowel corresponding to the long vowel of the etymon." [p. 8] "Furthermore, many grammatical concepts are expressed suprasegmentally (i.e. by vowel-length and pitch-accent)."

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Gorowa (qs-tier-2026-09-12) has an empty rule, so this is new material rather than confirmation: it supplies (a) an explicit 'pitch accent' label for Gorwaa/Iraqw and (b) a working assumption of penultimate stress in nativised Swahili loans. Both statements are made jointly for Gorwaa and Iraqw.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No dedicated stress section. In the loanword-phonology discussion the authors treat the penultimate syllable as 'the stressed syllable' (Swahili loans get their penult vowel lengthened there, and a stressed long final vowel is disallowed and repaired with -ʔV), while in the morphology section they characterise Gorwaa and Iraqw as marking grammatical categories 'suprasegmentally (i.e. by vowel-length and pitch accent)'. The 'stressed (penultimate)' remarks are made about Swahili etyma being nativised, where Swahili's own penultimate stress and the adapted form coincide, so they do not amount to a clean statement of native Gorwaa word-stress placement; the explicit typological label the paper gives the language is pitch accent plus contrastive vowel length.
new_statements.exceptions: Ex. 11d [mta:] 'block, neighbourhood' keeps a long final vowel unrepaired ('But:'). Antepenult vowel deletion (exx. 8-9) is optional and attributed to speaker variation / recency of borrowing, not to phonological structure.
new_statements.identity_note: Gorwaa is the author's spelling of Gorowa (goro1270), spoken in Babati District, Manyara Region, Tanzania. Harvey & Mreta 2016 describe Gorwaa and its close relative Iraqw (iraq1241) together and make the pitch accent and penult-stress statements jointly for both; no dialect of Gorwaa is singled out.

tone_statements.quote: Suprasegmentally, all Southern Cushitic1 languages have a pitch-accent-system that works on the morphosyntactic level primarily. ... whereas in Iraqw and Gorwaa it bears a considerable functional load, with the marked tone (accent 2) operating in extensive parts of the grammar. ... In contrast to Alagwa and Burunge, Iraqw and Gorwaa exploit the tonal contrast to a much larger extent. First, both of them also utilize the tone opposition in nominal derivational suffixes, as shown in (8-9).

tone_statements.summary: Pitch accent: unmarked accent 1 (level low) vs marked accent 2 (H on final syllable of the phonological word), mostly grammatical; stated jointly for Iraqw and Gorwaa; stress rule quoted is Iraqw's.

tone_statements.quote: For many Cushitic languages, there is no obligatoriness of one stressed (or high-toned) syllable per word. Hyman (2006) argues that such languages are not stress languages but tone languages, where providing prominence is realised by pitch. This is at least valid for Somali, 'Afar, all of Southern Cushitic, Arbore, Konso, Oromo, Awngi, and Bilin. In the Southern Cushitic languages, the majority of the nouns are toneless and only receive tone through suffixation of high-toned morphemes - see Mous (1993: 21) for Iraqw, Harvey (2018: 76-79) for Gorwaa, Mous (2016: 21) for Alagwa, and Kießling (1994: 25-28) for Burunge.
tone_statements.locator: Section 3 'Properties of Cushitic grammar-only tone languages', opening paragraph
tone_statements.n_tones: Privative H vs toneless (grammatical H from suffixes)

readall_conflicts: Within Harvey & Mreta 2016 there is a tension rather than a contradiction: the loanword sections speak of 'the stressed (i.e. penultimate) syllable' and of a ban on 'a stressed final vowel which is long', while the morphology section calls the prosodic system 'vowel-length and pitch accent'. The penultimate remarks are about adapted Swahili words (whose etyma are penult-stressed), so they are weak evidence for a native Gorwaa fixed: penultimate syllable stress rule; the pitch accent label is the direct statement about the language. The listed target (Harvey 2020 webinar) could not be read, so no second source was available to resolve it.
